title: Rethinking Message Passing Neural Networks with Diffusion Distance-guided Stress Majorization

problem.claim: Existing message passing neural networks face severe over-smoothing and over-correlation issues associated with their objective and neighborhood aggregation operations.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes DDSM, an MPNN model based on stress majorization and orthogonal regularization to address over-smoothing and over-correlation.
The paper introduces diffusion distances into the framework to guide message passing operations and develops efficient distance-approximation algorithms supported by theoretical analyses.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that DDSM consistently and considerably outperforms 15 strong baselines on homophilic and heterophilic graphs.

narrative_sequence.summary: MPNNs are established models for learning on graph-structured data.
Many MPNNs suffer from over-smoothing and over-correlation linked to their objective and aggregation operations.
DDSM combines stress majorization and orthogonal regularization in an optimization framework.
Diffusion distances guide message passing, with efficient approximation algorithms and theoretical analyses.
Experiments compare DDSM with 15 baselines across homophilic and heterophilic graphs.

source_observation.claim: The proposed model combines stress majorization, orthogonal regularization, and diffusion-distance guidance to address known message-passing issues.

interpretation.claim: An optimization framework can be used to redesign message passing around geometric constraints and distance information.

application.claim: When designing graph neural networks, consider explicit regularization and diffusion-based structural signals to mitigate over-smoothing and over-correlation.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish which component is responsible for the reported performance or how the approach behaves outside the stated graph settings.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, tasks, evaluation metrics, or experimental settings.
The abstract does not report numerical performance results or ablation findings.
The abstract does not detail the theoretical results or distance-approximation algorithms.
